rounds.response: Aim: characterize how graduate students use AI tools during literature reviews—prevalence, typical workflows, effects on search/synthesis behavior and perceived trust/risks—and test whether AI-assisted workflows produce different review artifacts. Design/justification: a rapid mixed-methods study (broad cross-sectional online survey for prevalence and predictors, purposive subsample of semi-structured interviews + artifact comparison of short review products; optional lightweight digital-trace logs if participants consent) that leverages your existing survey items and grant measures for fast instrument development and is feasible within six weeks. Main work packages: (A) draft survey & instrument mapping from shared-drive materials; (B) expedited IRB/consent template and recruitment plan; (C) survey deployment and monitoring; (D) recruit and conduct 15–20 interviews and collect 20–30 short review artifacts (AI-assisted vs non-assisted); (E) quantitative analysis (descriptives, regressions), qualitative coding, artifact quality comparison; (F) write methods/results outline for conference submission. Timeline/milestones (6 weeks): Week 1—finalize measures, IRB submission, prep recruitment; Week 2—launch survey; Week 3—close survey, begin interviews/artifact collection; Weeks 4–5—complete interviews, clean data, run analyses; Week 6—draft and finalize conference submission. Immediate next step I will do now: draft the survey instrument and a one-page IRB/consent summary from the shared-drive materials for your quick review.

rounds.response:
1) Aims & research questions — 1. Estimate prevalence/patterns of graduate students’ use of AI for literature reviews; 2. Describe common AI-assisted workflows, tool types, and perceived benefits/risks (trust, accuracy, efficiency); 3. Test associations between AI-use patterns and self-reported confidence/effort/quality proxies; 4. (Deferred if needed) Pilot a tiny artifact comparison only if time allows.  
2) Design summary — 1. Core: single cross-sectional online survey using adapted items from the shared-drive materials; 2. Brief embedded open-ended items for rapid qualitative insight (no large interview burden); 3. Use a very small purposive interview sample (3–4) only if survey response and RA time permit; 4. Artifact/think-aloud and trace logging moved to deferred/future work.  
3) Tasks / work packages (RA time budget ~0.3 FTE ≈ 12 hrs/week; PI to cover time-intensive tasks): 1) Instrument finalization — map shared-drive items, RA drafts survey (8–10 hrs first week), PI reviews/edits; 2) Ethics & consent — RA assembles packet (4–6 hrs), PI submits/signs; 3) Deployment & recruitment — PI sends endorsement email, RA (monitoring only: ~4–6 hrs/week) runs reminders and tracks response; 4) Data handling & analysis — RA performs scripted data cleaning and basic descriptives (spread over Weeks 3–4, ~12–15 hrs total), PI runs/regresses and writes interpretation; 5) Write-up for submission — PI drafts methods/results, RA prepares tables/figures (final ~8–10 hrs).  
4) Week-by-week schedule (4 weeks to deadline; assignable actions): Week 1 — finalize survey draft from shared-drive (RA drafts 8–10 hrs; PI reviews and finalizes), prepare/submit expedited IRB (RA compiles, PI signs); Week 2 — survey launch (PI sends recruitment email), RA monitors daily (~3–4 hrs total this week) and schedules reminders; Week 3 — mid-collection push and close survey end of Week 3 (RA sends reminder, PI posts in dept channels), if feasible conduct up to 3 short interviews (PI/RA split); Week 4 — data cleaning, primary analyses, rapid coding of open-ends (RA runs cleaning/scripts ~10–12 hrs, PI runs regressions and drafts submission text), finalize figures/tables and submit.  
Deferred / future work (do not attempt this term unless extra capacity): expanded qualitative interviews (6–8), formal artifact comparisons, and any digital-trace logging; immediate next step: RA to produce the first survey draft from shared-drive items today for PI review so IRB can be submitted early in Week 1.

rounds.response:
RA should (1) run and document the pre-specified regression models linking AI-use categories to core outcomes (confidence, perceived quality, time/effort), include key covariates, and run one robustness check for missingness/selection; (2) produce final descriptive tables and 2–3 publication-ready figures (prevalence bars, coefficient plot, theme-frequency chart) with short captions and exportable data; (3) rapid-code the open-ended survey responses using a small codebook (6–8 codes), report theme frequencies and 2–3 exemplar quotes per theme; (4) deliver reproducible analysis scripts (R/Stata), a one-page methods appendix describing measures/coding rules, and a brief README of any deviations.  

For the paper’s methodological contribution, pitch: (a) a practical, reproducible template for rapid mixed-methods assessment of emergent tool adoption (short core survey + embedded open-ends) suitable for low-resource, short-deadline settings; (b) a compact measurement battery for AI-assisted literature-review workflows adapted from existing departmental items, showing feasibility and face validity; (c) an efficiency-focused analytic pipeline demonstrating how rigorous descriptive/regression analysis plus rapid qualitative coding yields actionable methodological insights under ~0.3 FTE constraints; (d) explicit staging guidance that frames artifact/think-aloud work as deferred, providing a clear roadmap for more labor-intensive extensions.

variable_fidelity_rationale: Ethical constraint strictness: The constraints text emphasizes compliance with law, avoiding clearly harmful practices, and flagging ethical issues, which is somewhat more structured than a purely ‘minimal ethics’ reminder, though still not very stringent.

Data governance rules: The guidance to treat sensitive/identifiable data with caution and prefer de-identified data is somewhat more concrete than truly ‘informal rules,’ but still lacks rigid, formalized procedures.
Supervisor monitoring: The PI checks in multiple times with detailed, structured requests and feedback, which fits better with ‘periodic check’ than with a truly ‘hands off’ supervisor.

Deviation penalty: Consequences for misalignment are framed mainly as reduced trust and reliance rather than clear sanctions or task reassignment; this is closer to low-to-moderate penalty than a clearly ‘moderate’ one but still within its spirit.

overall_validity.rationale: Nearly all key variables and rules are instantiated faithfully: the fixed, non-movable deadline and medium-stakes opportunity are consistently reflected; resource updates occur via added documents at plausible intervals; actor behavior matches the specified low-frequency PI and grants officer interactions plus limited RA availability; and consequences for behavior align with moderate, non-catastrophic evaluation shifts rather than extreme sanctions. The rendering instructions are closely followed, with explicit consequence, context, resource, and actor updates each round, realistic event-based descriptions, no fourth-wall breaks, and coherent temporal continuity. Minor mismatches—such as supervision looking more like ‘periodic check’ than fully ‘hands off,’ and constraints/data governance being slightly more structured than ‘minimal’/‘informal’—are subtle and do not materially alter how the hypothesized constructs would influence the agent’s behavior. Because these deviations are small and peripheral to the central dynamics of deadline pressure, autonomy, task specificity, and resource/actor structure, the simulation provides a highly valid test of behavior under the intended configuration.
